I could have been lying in 6in water, with a broken leg and an 80 year old man trying to reach me.

Author: @stankbeans
Content:
I was right smack dab in the middle of the natural disaster area for Hurricane Helene, and would never wish that hell on anyone. 13 tornadoes in my small town spawned from the winds, and splintered thousands of electrical lines (I literally didn't see a standing power lines left in the county), and destroyed _hundreds_ of homes, leaving my wife and I trapped, due to how our driveway was cut out with trees on both sides, with the house just being in the middle of the woods. Hundreds of _large_ trees folded in on the driveway, and we had both been through 30 straight years of Hurricane warnings with nothing significant happening, so we stupidly didn't prepare at all. 
We ended up army crawling through thorny vines for 3 hours to try to find a neighbor to help, and there was.. well, no one. No phone service to call 911 with. The entire neighborhood's belongings are spread out over 2 miles, no water, no electricity, and _very little_ non-perishable food.  
  
It's a scary feeling, when you feel for the first time that you're _actually_ alone and there's not a soul to be reached who can help, since the roads could'nt be driven on due to the sheer amount of trees and shit on them.  
 
It took 3 months to regain electricity, and it was 100° outside a lot days. Hardest thing I've ever been through, and I hope nothing ever beats it.

Author: @R-U-1004
Content:
For those wondering why the hotel let you book for a forecasted disaster day:
1. The peak day of the disaster might change. So does the hotel need to close for lets say 1 week? There is also a problem with bookings that have existed loong time ago, or bookings that hotels do not have direct contacts with the guests, also can't directly cancel it (most 3rd party booking). Abruptly close and cancel all reservations is just another recipe for disaster.
2. Not all guests flew/travel in. Some might be locals.
3. Some also long stay guests. 
4. Can't say that all hotels do this, but mostly will give leniency if you wish to cancel/reschedule due to natural disasters. Even for non-refundable bookings.
5. Hotels trust that the guests are sound minded people that are capable of making their own logical decisions, instead of checking every personal details such as address, transportation methods, travel reasons, economic stability etc just to help them make a schedule. Hotels are hotels, not personal assistants.

Content:
Katrina hit as a Cat 3 with 125-mph winds - but it was a larger storm than Melissa. Cat 5 was in the middle of the Gulf.  Storms in the Gulf tend to lose strength at they approach land both due to frictional losses as well as the fact that the waters, while very warm, aren't deep and, thus, cannot sustain such intensity unless there is sufficient forward speed.  Melissa didn't have this problem because the waters off Jamaica are very deep.  That's (in addition to low shear and high pressure aloft) why it maintained intensity despite churning the Caribbean for days. 

Those X's on the windows won't do jack other than give a false sense of security.  I'm kind of surprised they don't have impact-resistant windows being where they're located.  Their distaster plan is awful.  That said, on the second floor I wouldn't really worry about it, except for gravel off the roof and that will shatter those panes with little difficulty.

I went to Disney World in September 2017 even though I knew Hurricane Irma was going to pass over Orlando during the trip.  I was getting there a few days before the parks were closed for two days and leaving several days after.

I had no competition for the front bench on the Liberty Belle(RIP), most rides on the days before the storm were essentially walk ons, and I wasn't sweating buckets when outside before the storm.  It was extra muggy on the first two days after the closures.

So many people rescheduled or canceled their flights that I had no neighbors on any of my four flights.  On one flight, everybody could have their own row if they wanted.  Only one couple didn't take that offer.

Irma was a category 1 by the time it got to Orlando, although the winds were still quite damaging.  Disney World's hotels can withstand at least a category 3.  I knew I would be safe.  Locals evacuate to Disney World during hurricanes.  The campgrounds, both tent/RV sites and cabins, were evacuated, along with the treehouse villas at a different hotel.

I was staying at French Quarter.  A hanging exit sign was ripped off the ceiling, lots of leaves and small branches were on the ground or in the bushes, more than one tree was heavily damaged but still standing, and at least one large tree was uprooted and on its side.  Sidewalks weren't blocked if you were capable of walking.  The branches were easy to step over.

Some water got into my room under the door, but the rolled up bath towel soaked up most of it.  The rest was in the carpet immediately adjacent to the door.  Those rooms no longer have carpet.  

I didn't post about my trip online before, during, or after.  I have no desire to chase clout.  I try to stay out of the spotlight as much as I possibly can.  I will go the long way around, even if it is extremely inconvenient, if I see a video camera.  I will just wait off to the side for still pictures, however, I won't try to hide rolling my eyes if they are posing in front of that godforsaken purple wall.
